title: Infection-acquired protection against SARS-CoV-2 infection and clinical severity by number of prior infections

paper_content.abstract:
SARS-CoV-2 reinfections have increased since Omicron and are common. Yet, as we approach
endemicity, the frequency, severity, and consequences of reinfections remain poorly understood. Using
data from a household transmission study in Managua, Nicaragua (2020-2024), we evaluated protection
conferred by one, two, and three+ prior infections and compared the severity of first, second, and third+
RT-PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections. Compared to those with no prior infections, one, two, and
three+ prior infections were associated with increasing protection from symptomatic infection, with
incidence rate ratios of 0.39, (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.26-0.61), 0.24 (95%CI: 0.13-0.42), and 0.20
(95%CI: 0.09-0.42), respectively. Among RT-PCR-confirmed infections, reinfections were associated with
decreased severity; compared with first infections, second infections had 1.57 (95%CI: 1.15-2.16) times
the proportion of subclinical disease and 0.65 (95%CI: 0.49-0.86) times the proportion of
moderate/severe disease. Our findings suggest that protection generated from two prior infections may
be stronger than one prior infection, although additional benefit beyond the second infection was not
clearly observed. Together, our results suggest we are approaching an endemic phase of SARS-CoV-2
characterized by reduced severity relative to first infections, yet the burden remains high, underscoring
the importance of maintaining immunity to manage ongoing disease.
paper_content.introduction:
It is still unclear what endemic SARS-CoV-2 will look like and whether future infections and disease will
differ from today. Population immunity continues to build through repeated infection and vaccination,
yet the virus keeps evolving, complicating efforts to achieve protection. Additionally, variant severity has
changed over time, with some pre-Omicron variants associated with increased severity and Omicron
with decreased severity.1 Although substantial literature exists on protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection,
our study addresses a gap by leveraging detailed infection histories in a cohort setting to examine the
associations of between repeated infections, protection and severity. In this work, we use data from a
community-based prospective cohort study in Nicaragua, a setting with high infection and vaccination
rates that is likely close to a stable level of endemicity. We measure the protection associated with prior
infection by comparing SARS-CoV-2 incidence among individuals with one, two, and three+ prior
infections, and we compare the severity of first, second, and third+ SARS-CoV-2 infections.
paper_content.results:
Between March 2020 and December 2023, 2,388 people aged 0-95 years (median age of 17 years)
participated in the Household Influenza Cohort Study (HICS) contributing a total of 8,947 person-years
(PY) of follow-up (Supplementary Table 1). Sex distribution was balanced among children, but adult male
participation was lower (Supplementary Figure 2). In Nicaragua, the original SARS-CoV-2 strain circulated
in 2020, Gamma and Delta predominated in 2021, and Omicron became dominant starting in 20222,3.
ELISA completeness was high, with blood samples available for an average of 95% of enrolled
participants during sampling times (Supplementary Table 2).

We detected a total of 3,644 serologically- or RT-PCR-confirmed infections among HICS participants.
Only 2 RT-PCR-detected infections were missing any symptom data; these 2 participants were excluded
from analyses, leaving a total of 3,642 infections. Over the course of their enrollment, 1,056 participants
(44.2%) had one detected infection, 782 (32.7%) two infections, 324 (13.6%) three+ infections, and 226
(9.5%) had no detected infections (Supplementary Table 1). The majority of those remaining uninfected
either left the cohort in 2020/2021 (n=164, 71.3%) or were enrolled as infants (n=32, 13.9%). By October
2021, 91.3% of HICS participants had been infected, and by October 2024, 97.7% had been infected
(Figure 1A). This population also experienced a high rate of reinfections, even before Omicron, with
16.6% of the population experiencing a reinfection by the end of 2021 and 58.9% by October 2024
(Supplementary Table 1).

Of the 3,642 total infections with symptom data, 1,145 (31.4%) were detected by RT-PCR. Among the
1,145 RT-PCR-confirmed infections, 346 were first, 615 were second, and 184 were third+ infections
(Figure 2A&B). The majority of RT-PCR-detected infections were subclinical or mild (75.5%), but 19.8%
were moderate and 4.6% were severe. We observed 6 SARS-CoV-2-associated deaths.

Nicaragua did not have access to vaccines as early as many other parts of the world. When vaccines did
become more widely available around September-October 2021, they included a broader selection of
lesser-studied SARS-CoV-2 vaccines 4. A large-scale vaccination effort followed, and by January 2022,
70.0% of HICS participants had been vaccinated (78.5% of adults, Figure 1B).

Protection from reinfection increased with the number of prior infections, and somewhat with the
severity of the outcome (all RT-PCR-confirmed, symptomatic, and moderate/severe infections), although
confidence intervals were wider for more severe outcomes. The highest protection was observed in
those with three+ prior infections against moderate/severe disease (0.19, 95%CI: 0.05-0.79), and the
lowest protection—0.52 (95%CI: 0.36-0.76)—was against all RT-PCR-confirmed infections in those with
one prior infection versus uninfected individuals (Figure 1 & Supplemental Tables 3&5).

The incidence of symptomatic infections was 14.1, 9.2, 5.9, and 4.8 cases per 100 PY for those with 0,
1, 2, and 3+ prior infections (Figure 1C), corresponding to incidence rate ratios (IRRs) of 0.39 (95%CI: 0.26-
0.61), 0.24 (0.13-0.42), and 0.20 (0.09-0.42) for those with 1, 2, and 3+ versus no prior infections (Figure
1D). For moderate/severe disease, incidence was 5.4, 2.8, 1.9, and 1.2 cases per 100 PY in those with 0,
1, 2, and 3+ prior infections, corresponding to IRRs of 0.26 (95%CI: 0.12-0.57), 0.23 (0.08-0.66), and 0.19
(0.05-0.79) for those with 1, 2, and 3+ versus 0 prior infections.

To further assess whether additional prior infections provided incremental protection, we compared
participants with ≥1 and ≥2 prior infections (Supplemental Figure 3). As shown in Supplemental Figure 3
A.1 & A.2, participants with two or more prior infections had significantly lower risk of RT-PCR-
confirmed infection compared to those with only one prior infection (IRRs of 0.61 [0.48-0.77] for 2 vs 1;
and 0.41 [0.26-0.63] for 3+ vs 1); protection also remained significant for 3+ vs 2 prior infections (IRR:
0.60 [0.38-0.93]). Similarly, we observed reduced risk of symptomatic infection for participants with 2 or
3+ infections compared to those with one (IRRs: 0.61 [0.46-0.82] and 0.47 [0.28-0.78], respectively).
However, the number of prior infections was not significantly associated with the risk of moderate or
severe disease (e.g. IRR for 2 vs 1 prior infection: 0.86 [0.52-1.44]) or symptomatic infection when
restricting to participants with ≥2 prior infections (IRR: 0.81 [0.48-1.34]). These findings suggest that
multiple prior infections enhance protection against reinfection, although these associations are weaker
and less precise when examining more severe outcomes.

Similarly, reinfections were less severe than first infections (Figure 2 & Supplemental Tables 4&6),
though with no apparent additional benefit from increasing number of prior infections as seen with
protection from infection. The proportion of moderate/severe disease decreased from 31.5% to 21.5%
to 21.2% in first, second, and third+ infections (Figure 2B), corresponding to relative severities of 0.65
(95%CI: 0.49-0.86) and 0.70 (95%CI: 0.45-1.09) for second and third+ versus first infections (Figure 2C).
Meanwhile, the proportion of subclinical infections increased from 17.3% to 29.9% to 31.0% in first,
second, and third+ infections, corresponding to increased relative severities of 1.57 (95%CI: 1.15-2.16)
and 1.71 (95%CI: 1.11-2.62) for second and third+ infections versus first infections.

Because there are many potentially confounding factors, and for transparency, we have included
Supplemental Figure 4, which shows partially and alternately adjusted models for the main protection
and severity analyses. While all models produced qualitatively similar point estimates indicating
protection, not all models yielded statistically significant associations. In particular, when time since
prior infection or vaccination was included as a covariate, confidence intervals widened and some
estimates were no longer statistically significant (Supplemental Figure S4). For severity analyses,
estimates remained generally similar across model specifications. This stability suggests that variables
that confound infection risk (such as time since infection or vaccination) are not strong confounders of
severity in our community-based cohort once infection has occurred. Additional adjustment for these
variables increased uncertainty (wider confidence intervals) without materially changing the point
estimates, so the simpler model was retained for the main severity analyses.

Stratifying by year (Supplemental Figure 5), we again observed increasing protection with each
subsequent reinfection for 2021 and 2022, however incidence was much lower in 2023 and 2024, and
there were so few first infections in those years that we did not observe protection for 2023 or 2024
(Supplemental Figure 5 & Supplemental Table 7). Reductions in disease severity were apparent in the
pre-Omicron period, but not during Omicron (Supplemental Figure 6 & Supplemental Table 8). During
the pre-Omicron period, second infections were associated with 0.56 (95%CI: 0.40-0.79) times as much
moderate/severe disease and 1.95 (95%CI: 1.33-2.85) times more subclinical infections versus first
infections.

Additionally, the period-of- and time-since- last infection were associated with protection from
reinfection, and, to a lesser extent, severity (Supplemental Figure 7). As expected, protection was
highest when the prior infection matched the circulating variant, and was more recent. Looking at
period of last infection, the highest protection was observed in the pre-Omicron period for those with a
prior pre-Omicron infection (IRR: 0.04, 95%CI: 0.02-0.09 for symptomatic infection) and in the Omicron
era for those with a prior Omicron infection (IRR: 0.06, 95%CI: 0.04-0.09 for any PCR-confirmed
infection). For time since last infection, protection was highest pre-Omicron, for those whose last
infection was 0-180 days prior (IRR of 0.02, 95%CI: 0.00-0.11 for moderate/severe infection). Protection
remained present even for participants with original SARS-CoV-2 infections and infections ≥1 year prior.
For example, during the pre-Omicron era, protection against symptomatic infection for participants with
an original SARS-CoV-2 infection, the IRR was 0.31 (95%CI: 0.25-0.40), and for those with an infection 1-
2 years prior, the IRR was 0.59 (95%CI: 0.45- 0.78). We cannot explain the observed increase in
protection among people with prior infections ≥2 years earlier compared to with those infected 1-2
years earlier, though this may reflect chance variation, differences in variants, or selection effects such
as survivor bias, where those with more durable immunity (e.g., better mucosal immunity) remain
uninfected for longer.

Protection results were largely similar for age groups 18+, 10-17, and 0-9 years (Supplemental Figure 8),
with weaker associations for the youngest children. Likewise, relative severity of reinfection
(Supplemental Figure 9) was similar for adults and older children, but there was no association for the
youngest children.
paper_content.methods:
Ethics Statement
This study was approved by the institutional review boards at the Nicaraguan Ministry of Health and the
University of Michigan (HUM00119145 and HUM00178355 and CIRE code # NIC-MINSA/CNDR CIRE-
05/04/17-080 Rev 13). Informed consent or parental permission was obtained for all participants.
Assent was obtained from children aged ≥6 years.

The Household Influenza Cohort Study (HICS)
HICS is an ongoing household cohort study with an embedded household transmission study, located in
district II of Managua, Nicaragua. The neighborhoods in district II range from low to middle class,
including several areas classified as urban slums. It was started in 2017 to study influenza, and in 2020
SARS-CoV-2 was added. Regular blood samples are collected for all cohort participants, twice yearly in
2020 and 2021, then yearly thereafter. The transmission study is activated when a household member
becomes sick and tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR after seeking care at the study health clinic.
Activated households are visited by study staff regularly, at approximately days 0, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 30,
for collection of respiratory samples and symptom diaries from all household members, regardless of
symptoms.

Laboratory Assays
Blood samples were tested as paired serum samples (current vs baseline) using an enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) protocol adapted from the Krammer laboratory 20. The SARS-CoV-2 spike
receptor binding domain (RBD), spike, and nucleoprotein (NP) proteins for ELISAs were produced in
single batches at the Life Sciences Institute at the University of Michigan; these were generated based
on the original SARS-CoV-2 strain. RBD was used for screening (positive/negative) as it is more specific
than spike, and spike was used to titer samples that screened positive by RBD ELISA; NP ELISAs were also
run, to distinguish between vaccine and infection responses. Real-time reverse-transcription polymerase
chain reaction (RT-PCR) was performed according to the protocol from Chu et al. 21.
All RT-PCR and most ELISAs were performed at the Nicaraguan National Virology Laboratory, with a
minority of 2020 annual samples processed at the University of Michigan.

Infection histories
We used positive serology screens, antibody titer values, 4-fold rises in titer, and RT-PCR positivity to
define first and secondary infections, as outlined in Supplemental Figure 1. To be defined as an
infection, serological samples must have been from participants at least 6 months of age, to avoid
incorrectly classifying maternal immunity, and first infections serologically detected by RBD screen or
spike titer must have been before the first COVID vaccination. We estimated the date of serologically-
defined infections to be the median between samples, or for positive screens, we used the median of
the sample date and March 1, 2020 or the participant’s birthday if they were born after 2020 or a
previous negative sample date. RT-PCR-detected infections must have been ≥60 days apart from each
other. Infection sequences based on serology were required to have a longer time span between
infections than those involving a PCR-detected infection given the inherent uncertainty in the exact
timing of serologically-detected infections. Distinct infections detected serologically must have been ≥6
months apart from each other. Paired serology samples that spanned a vaccination event or were
collected soon after vaccination were excluded, as the resulting antibody rise likely reflects vaccine-
induced immunity rather than infection. Sequential infections detected by RT-PCR and 4-fold rise must
have occurred >90 days apart from each other. Any potential infections within 60 days of each other
were flagged for manual inspection.

Severity
Severity was evaluated only for RT-PCR-confirmed infections, as symptom diaries and clinic records were
only available exclusively for these infections. Symptoms reported in daily symptom diaries and clinic
visits were used to define severity, as severe (hospitalized, doctors say they should have been
hospitalized, or death), moderate (lower respiratory symptoms or overall poor condition), mild (loss of
smell/taste, fever, or ≥2 symptoms), or subclinical (≤1 symptom not meeting definitions for higher
severity).

Main Exposures and Outcomes
For protection analyses, all prior infections detected serologically and by RT-PCR were used to define the
exposure, and the outcome was incident RT-PCR-detected infections with defined severity. Severity
analyses were restricted to RT-PCR-detected infections only; the exposure for severity analyses was
infection number (1st, 2nd, 3rd+), and the outcome was severity.

Vaccination
Vaccines (Covishield 19) were available to elderly or high-risk individuals starting in early 2021. In the fall
of 2021, vaccinations became much more widely available, including Sputnik V, Sputnik Light,
AstraZeneca, Abdala, Soberana, Pfizer, Janssen, Sinopharm, and Moderna. Vaccination status was
defined as unvaccinated, partially vaccinated, fully vaccinated (number of doses varied by vaccine;
Sputnik light only required one dose for full vaccination), or boosted; we counted vaccines that occurred
at least 14 days prior. Vaccines targeting the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid were not counted with the
vaccinated groups (only a few people have had a vaccine targeting the nucleocapsid, starting in 2023).

Analysis
While new households were recruited in 2023 to maintain the cohort size, participants were limited to
those enrolled before January 1, 2021 or were born into the cohort (enrolled before age 1y) so that full
infection histories would be known. Person-time, for the protection analysis, included all weeks in the
study period when participants were enrolled, excluding the period immediately following infection. We
excluded up to 52 days post-infection, as this was the shortest interval at which a new infection was
detected in the cohort due to our infection definition. Person-time for an individual changed exposure
categories as new immune events occurred.
Poisson regression and mixed effect Poisson regression models were used to calculate relative risks (RR),
using the glm (base R) and glmer (lme4 package version 1.1-37) functions in R. Percent protection was
calculated as (1- RR)*100. We stratified all analyses by age (0-9y, 10-17y, and 18+y). We also stratified
by year or period, to account for high vaccination rates starting around November 2021 and differences
in variants.

Covariates
For model adjustment, we considered vaccination status (none, partial, full, and boosted), age (in years),
sex, days since last infection and vaccination (both categorized as ‘uninfected/unvaccinated’, [0-14),
[14-49) [vaccination only], then increments of 60 days until [870-2000]), year or period (original SARS-CoV-2,
pre-Omicron variant, and Omicron), and household clustering (as a mixed effect). Not all variables could
be included in stratified analyses. Examples of model specification are shown in Supplementary Tables 3
& 4.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I have reviewed the paper by Maier et al. on SARS-CoV-2 infections and have the following major and minor comments and suggestions to the authors:
* Major comments
1. A general limitation of the analysis is that it does not account for sex, and age, which are known to be two key determinants of disease outcome. Additionally, household clustering is probably also important to account for in order for the statistical inference to be correct.
2. The conclusion that protection from prior infection was stronger pre-Omicron (line 126) must be backed up by a formal statistical interaction analysis.
3. If conclusions specific to children are to be included (line 126-128), they should be backed up by formal statistical analysis and be based on results presented in the main text.
4. The number of reinfections during the periods before Omicron seems surprisingly high compared with similar studies, also given the high protection from prior infections that were reported for the present cohort. The authors should comment on this unexpected finding. Is one possible explanation the late roll out of vaccines?
5. Selection issues should be discussed as a potential, partial explanation for the observed increase in protection from prior infection. How large was the case fatality in the cohort? Even with low case fatality, the reinfected could still represent a group of less susceptible individuals or of less need of shelter against exposure. Is it possible to investigate the association between prior severity of infection and outcome of next infection?
* Minor comments
1. The paper lacks a standard Table 1 with descriptive data on the HICS cohort
2. The abstract lacks clear conclusions of the type formulated in the first paragraph of the Discussion (line 125-128).
3. Much of the reporting is focused on adults (age 18+), I would suggest that also the supplementary tables is stratified so that results for adults are presented in separate tables.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
General
This is a research article by Dr. Maier and colleagues comparing the protection of infection-acquired immunity from single vs multiple prior infections against symptomatic infection and clinical severity. The study concludes that infection-acquired immunity against symptomatic infection increases with each subsequent infection and that clinical severity declines with each subsequent infection. The study leverages a household cohort study from Managua, Nicaragua collecting routine serologic testing and symptom-triggered PCR testing over the entire Covid-19 pandemic period (2000-2024). This cohort design and dataset is an impressive strength of the article, given the complete individual histories of vaccination and prior infection based on the longitudinal design; this level of detailed data is rare. However, the current analytic structure has some methodological issues that preclude meaningful interpretation of the study findings in their present form. First, the analysis does not appear to account for timing since the last infection – however we know infection-acquired immunity wanes. This results in downward biasing of the estimate for protection generated by a single infection (which has a longer period of follow up, presumably after substantial waning of protection) compared to protection generated by a second or third infection (with shorter period of follow up, presumably during a period of higher protection before waning). Second, the findings of lower clinical severity from repeated infections could also be explained by both differences in which variants are circulating during 1st vs 2nd vs 3rd infection (and variant-specific clinical severity) and not accounting for waning of protection. Third, there may be differential indirect protection on the household level that is affecting these direct protection estimates. As the number of prior infections increases, so does the immunity of the household members, which may confound measure of direct protection (providing more indirect protection over time in households with members with higher number of prior infections, which could confound the direct protection measures). Finally, the statistical analysis and data processing could be more clearly described to better understand the analysis. I hope my comments can be constructive, as most of my concerns can be addressed and the scientific question and study are both important and interesting.
Major
--Accounting for timing since last infection / waning in protection: It is well established that protection from infection-acquired immunity wanes over time, whether due to immune-mediated mechanisms or due to increasing mismatch of host immune response and evolving viral variants. Therefore, an analysis comparing protection from different numbers of infections needs to account for timing since last infection to account for this waning of protection. The current main analysis does not appear to do so, which will bias the estimates, especially for single infection persons that have a longer follow up period (likely with substantial waning of protection) compared to the two or three infection participants with a relatively shorter follow up period (where protection will be stronger). This is evidenced in the authors’ supplemental analysis. For example, a person with single infection induced protection may have their next infection up to >3 years later, compared to a participant with triple infection induced protection which would have their next infection within 1-2 years. Therefore, is the lower protection from single infection compared to multiple infections due to differences in the immunity or simply timing since last infection? This should be rigorously addressed to determine the validity of the study findings, which currently focus on number of infections rather than timing since last infection. This issue also affects the analysis on clinical severity, which may once again bias downwards protection from single infection due to not accounting for timing since the last infection. The authors could create categories of timing of their prior infection states or perform a more sophisticated rolling matching process (i.e., match 1 vs 0 prior infections over defined time period, match 2 vs 0 prior infections, etc). These proposed approaches each have some challenges (e.g., needing to have overlapping time periods between different immune statuses), but this concern can likely be mostly addressed with additional analysis and should be featured in the main analysis.
--Clinical severity analysis methodological questions: From the current analysis, it is not entirely clear whether clinical severity is lower due to the protection generated from multiple infections or due to the variants affecting these different prior infection groups (e.g., variants circulating when participants have 1 vs 2 vs 3 infections are different). This is partially addressed by their pre- and post-omicron period analysis, but further work could be done to answer this question. As one potential approach, the authors could perform rolling matching to follow matched participants over the same variant periods (ideally more fine scale than just pre- and post-omicron), while accounting for timing of prior infection and vaccine differences. Alternatively, the authors could also highlight this as a limitation (including in the Abstract) if the sample size does not permit. Furthermore, the abstract mentions only comparing clinical severity of PCR+ cases, however the authors should also account for any differences in the fraction of asymptomatic infection (given their serology data) between 1 vs 2 vs 3 prior infection to answer this question about clinical severity.
--Confounding from indirect protection: Prior studies have shown that both Covid-19 vaccines and infection-acquired immunity generate indirect protection, reducing risk of infection to nearby social contacts. The current analysis may be affected by this, given that cases with 3+ infections likely co-reside with household members with high immunity, which may falsely appear as higher direct protection to the case, whereas it’s actually due to the indirect protection from the household members. Given the impressive household cohort study done by the authors, this could be directly evaluated and accounted for in the analysis based on data availability.
--Description of methods: The methods section is a bit sparse, which makes it more challenging to follow. The following would help: formal specification of the statistical model, relevant covariates, definition of person-time, treatment of repeated individuals (same participant in different immune categories), censoring, data processing, relevant reporting checklists. Discussion on why the authors did not use time-to-event modeling and matching. Could the authors clarify when they use PCR+ only vs any infection (PCR or serology) in the analysis (only for clinical severity analysis?), as it’s a bit challenging to follow. Does subclinical infection refer to PCR+ case with only one symptom or serologic asymptomatic cases or both?
--Vaccination: There is very limited description of the vaccination of this population, which should be expanded. As above, timing of last vaccine should ideally be accounted for in all analyses.
--Sensitivity analysis: The main analysis focuses on “symptomatic infection” but do the results hold for any infection (asymptomatic + symptomatic)?
Minor
--Consider revised title, “Infection-acquired protection against SARS-CoV-2 symptomatic infection and clinical severity by number of prior infections”
--Abstract: Consider reporting relative risk rather than percentage increases.
--Writing: Would prepare an Introduction vs Results section, rather than a single section (which basically lacks an Introduction). I would consider reworking the Introduction to focus more on addressing prior literature and the key scientific gap this study aims to fill.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this interesting study.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Overview: This article examines the relationship between prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and subsequent COVID-19 disease severity outcomes. While the protective effect of prior infection is relatively well-established in existing literature, the manuscript's exploration of severity outcomes offers a somewhat more novel contribution. The authors effectively leverage an existing cohort in a high-transmission setting, which is a methodological strength. However, I have substantial concerns about the analytical approach that significantly undermine the validity of the findings. My primary reservations focus on two critical methodological components: (1) the calculation of person-time in the analysis, and (2) the absence of calendar time as a variable in the primary model (though a stratified version is included).
Abstract:
• I find the last sentence a bit confusing. Is this analysis among people who were infected and then you compared the risk of severity within those infected or was it a “protection” estimate looking at the overall risk of those severe disease presentations? While this is better explained in the main text, I would suggest re-writing the abstract to make it stand on its own a bit better.
Introduction: Generally, I think the introduction was lacking and doesn’t capture the existing knowledge quite as well as I would expect. Specifically:
• Is there evidence to suggest that there is a change in the severity of COVID-19 over time?
• How is the change in severity associated with changes in variants or the increase in immunity events?
• There is already literature about protection from prior infections in regards to likelihood of infection, symptomatic infections and severe outcomes. Within the literature that exists, where is the specific gap you are filling?
• Please delineate between the introduction and the results (assume this happened at line 42 based on information in the paragraph running from 43-49).
Results:
• Based on the methods it seems like you included serological infections as new infections but in the figures it looks like your outcome is PCR detected infections. So is serology-based infections for the exposure? For the rest of the review, I am assuming serology-based infections were specifically used for the exposure and PCR were the outcome. Please clarify this in the results and methods.
• Please define variant time periods in the legend for the variant specific periods.
• You observed an increase in protection among people >2 years since last infection relative to the 1-2 year group for all three outcomes, please explain.
Discussion/conclusion:
• I am not sure I fully agree with the statement that you have complete infection histories for each participant. Because of the serological data, you have better data than just clinical PCRs on prior infection data, but it seems possible that secondary infections were missed (ex. if a person didn’t come in for clinical testing for two infections within a 6-month window, my understanding is that they would be classified as one prior infection based on serology).
Methods: The study relies on an existing cohort of people and gets data from a combination of clinical and household data - which is a strength, but I have a few questions about how infections were captured and what infections were used in the analysis:
• Infection capture:
o Who are the respiratory samples collected for – mainly are household members tested during the visits? “Activated households are visited by study staff regularly, at approximately days 0, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 30, for collection of respiratory samples and symptom diaries.”
o For the secondary infections identified by serology, what dose “Must not surround vaccination” mean in regards to time?
o Why do you require the serological based first infection detection to be >=90 day prior to vaccination? I understand that after a vaccine, the serological testing may be misclassified but am not sure how it would be misclassified prior to the vaccination event.
o Why are some of the time gaps 90 days and some 180 days (6 months) for serology? Specifically, you state that the first to secondary infections detected through serology need to be 6 months apart (left side of S.figure 1) and that the first PCR infection to secondary serology-based infection need to be 90 days part?
o Generally confused on when the serologically defined infections were stated to have occurred. The day of the fold change >= 6 months after the last? This is specifically for the time since last event analysis.
• Person-time:
o Did you include person-time during the periods directly following prior infection, during which people were not “susceptible” to infections based on your definitions of new infections? If so, it seems like this may be driving part of the large amount of protection you observed from prior infections (person time included but outcomes not possible). Am I missing something?
• Accounting for calendar time in the analysis:
o Can you explain why you didn’t account for calendar time in your primary model – though I recognize you did a stratified version? If calendar time is not accounted for, I fear that some of the severity-based findings may be driven by what variants each exposure group (first, second, third prior infection) preceded. Even within the stratified analysis, I worry that calendar time may be confounding the association of interest.
o Also, because may COVID-19 symptoms are non-specific, I would be concerned that other circulating respiratory pathogens may contribute to the reported symptom burdens differently by time.
• Was the household correlation structure accounted for in the model? Or if it wasn’t, can you explain why not?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response To Reviewer Comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
I have reviewed the paper by Maier et al. on SARS-CoV-2 infections and have the following major and minor
comments and suggestions to the authors:
* Major comments
1. A general limitation of the analysis is that it does not account for sex, and age, which are known to
be two key determinants of disease outcome. Additionally, household clustering is probably also
important to account for in order for the statistical inference to be correct.
RESPONSE:
Thank you for the suggestion. We considered adjusting for all of the reviewer-suggested variables in both
the protection and severity models. In doing so, we compared AICs and likelihood ratio tests. We ended up
adjusting the protection analysis for vaccination, age, sex, times since last infection and vaccination,
calendar time, and household clustering. And we adjusted the severity analysis for vaccination, age, sex,
and calendar time; the additional variables made the model fit worse for the severity analysis, so they were
not included in the main analysis, but we did include a supplemental figure adjusted for time since infection

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
While the authors’ revision is appreciated, there are some remaining analytic and methodological issues that should be more fully addressed. Since some issues could affect the core study findings, these should be revised to ensure the conclusions are well supported by the data.
The study should more closely account for time since last infection/vaccination to ensure their findings are solid. (1) New Figure S9a (compared to Figure 2c) suggests that when accounting for time since last infection/vaccination, the results are no longer statistically significant in the severity analysis. Is that correct? If so, this would change the study conclusion to their observed relationship for severity being based on time since last infection/vaccine rather than the number of infections itself. (2) While the revised statistical adjustment including time since infection is a step in the right direction, the categories are also too broad (0-6 months, 6-12 months, 1-2 year, 2+ years). The observed difference between the protection due to different number of infections could be affected due to poor match for time since last infection within these categories. To determine if this is an issue, I would first perform a descriptive analysis to determine if there is a difference in average time since last infection / vaccine between those with a 1st vs 2nd vs 3rd infection. If there is imbalance, the authors should account for this (ideally with matching), but at a minimum, by a more finely tuned statistical adjustment. If no imbalance within these categories, then only my first comment remains.
The study’s conclusion is that higher protection and reduced severity of future SARS-CoV-2 infections are driven by higher infection-acquired protection from each subsequent infection. However, variant traits could equally explain these findings. Based on the statistical design, I do not think this can be disentangled, as simply pre-Omicron or Omicron is far too crude over a 4-year period. While the authors do mention this limitation, the Abstract, Discussion, and much of the manuscript do not sufficiently describe that both explanations are plausible. This should be revised.
Looking at Figure 1A, there is fairly limited overlap any 1st infection (0 gray) and 2+ (blue) / 3+ (dark blue) reinfections. Therefore, I’d be curious if only reinfections (1 prior infection, 2 prior infections, 3 prior infections) were included, and 1st infections were excluded, would the results hold. It would also lead to a better timing match and temporal match overall (see first comment).
The authors did not address the point of confounding due to indirect protection from household members, which is another plausible explanation for these findings. A random effects design would not address this. At the minimum, this should be highlighted as a key limitation, as it could undermine the study conclusions. Ideally, the authors could at least perform some descriptive analysis to investigate this if data is available.
Was the adjustment for calendar time just two periods (pre-Omicron vs Omicron) for 4 entire years? If so, “calendar time” is misleading and would suggest being more clear about what this represents, or revising this variable to be more temporally granular.
The use of AIC for variable selection is probably not the right approach for this casual inference analysis. The models adjusting for time since infection/vaccine should be the primary model.
From most of results, it’s not clear that 3rd infection vs 2nd infection are different. However, the authors conclusions focus on each infection yielding additional protection. This should be formally tested and interpreted as such.
It’s still unclear if the study demonstrates that protection against infection is increased (last sentence of abstract), rather just reduced symptomatic infections (i.e., the same rate of infection when accounting for sub-clinical infection may be present). My understanding is the majority of PCR tests are symptom-triggered, therefore the end point is symptomatic infection (not all infections), as most sub-clinical infections would be missed (since they would never be tested). Would appreciate clarification on this point.
I’m still not clear which analyses use inferred serologic infections (as outcome or exposure), and it seems that the explanations are conflicting in different parts of manuscript and response letter.
Most studies define reinfections as 90 days after the prior infection. Would this definition affect the results? Intermittent viral shedding and PCR positivity for weeks is common.
The study methods are still hard to follow.
The underlying data and study design is very strong, but the analysis and interpretation can hopefully be revised with these changes.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

SARS-CoV-2 reinfections have increased since Omicron and are common. Yet, as we approach
endemicity, the frequency, severity, and consequences of reinfections remain poorly understood. Using
data from a household transmission study in Managua, Nicaragua (2020-2024), we evaluated protection
conferred by one, two, and three+ prior infections and compared the severity of first, second, and third+
RT-PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infections. Compared to those with no prior infections, one, two, and
three+ prior infections were associated with increasing protection from symptomatic infection, with
incidence rate ratios of 0.39, (95% Confidence Interval [CI]: 0.26-0.61), 0.24 (95%CI: 0.13-0.42), and 0.20
(95%CI: 0.09-0.42), respectively. Among RT-PCR-confirmed infections, reinfections were associated with
decreased severity; compared with first infections, second infections had 1.57 (95%CI: 1.15-2.16) times
the proportion of subclinical disease and 0.65 (95%CI: 0.49-0.86) times the proportion of
moderate/severe disease. Our findings suggest that protection generated from two prior infections may
be stronger than one prior infection, although additional benefit beyond the second infection was not
clearly observed. Together, our results suggest we are approaching an endemic phase of SARS-CoV-2
characterized by reduced severity relative to first infections, yet the burden remains high, underscoring
the importance of maintaining immunity to manage ongoing disease.

---

## Introduction

It is still unclear what endemic SARS-CoV-2 will look like and whether future infections and disease will
differ from today. Population immunity continues to build through repeated infection and vaccination,
yet the virus keeps evolving, complicating efforts to achieve protection. Additionally, variant severity has
changed over time, with some pre-Omicron variants associated with increased severity and Omicron
with decreased severity.1 Although substantial literature exists on protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection,
our study addresses a gap by leveraging detailed infection histories in a cohort setting to examine the
associations of between repeated infections, protection and severity. In this work, we use data from a
community-based prospective cohort study in Nicaragua, a setting with high infection and vaccination
rates that is likely close to a stable level of endemicity. We measure the protection associated with prior
infection by comparing SARS-CoV-2 incidence among individuals with one, two, and three+ prior
infections, and we compare the severity of first, second, and third+ SARS-CoV-2 infections.

---

## Results

Between March 2020 and December 2023, 2,388 people aged 0-95 years (median age of 17 years)
participated in the Household Influenza Cohort Study (HICS) contributing a total of 8,947 person-years
(PY) of follow-up (Supplementary Table 1). Sex distribution was balanced among children, but adult male
participation was lower (Supplementary Figure 2). In Nicaragua, the original SARS-CoV-2 strain circulated
in 2020, Gamma and Delta predominated in 2021, and Omicron became dominant starting in 20222,3.
ELISA completeness was high, with blood samples available for an average of 95% of enrolled
participants during sampling times (Supplementary Table 2).

We detected a total of 3,644 serologically- or RT-PCR-confirmed infections among HICS participants.
Only 2 RT-PCR-detected infections were missing any symptom data; these 2 participants were excluded
from analyses, leaving a total of 3,642 infections. Over the course of their enrollment, 1,056 participants
(44.2%) had one detected infection, 782 (32.7%) two infections, 324 (13.6%) three+ infections, and 226
(9.5%) had no detected infections (Supplementary Table 1). The majority of those remaining uninfected
either left the cohort in 2020/2021 (n=164, 71.3%) or were enrolled as infants (n=32, 13.9%). By October
2021, 91.3% of HICS participants had been infected, and by October 2024, 97.7% had been infected
(Figure 1A). This population also experienced a high rate of reinfections, even before Omicron, with
16.6% of the population experiencing a reinfection by the end of 2021 and 58.9% by October 2024
(Supplementary Table 1).

Of the 3,642 total infections with symptom data, 1,145 (31.4%) were detected by RT-PCR. Among the
1,145 RT-PCR-confirmed infections, 346 were first, 615 were second, and 184 were third+ infections
(Figure 2A&B). The majority of RT-PCR-detected infections were subclinical or mild (75.5%), but 19.8%
were moderate and 4.6% were severe. We observed 6 SARS-CoV-2-associated deaths.

Nicaragua did not have access to vaccines as early as many other parts of the world. When vaccines did
become more widely available around September-October 2021, they included a broader selection of
lesser-studied SARS-CoV-2 vaccines 4. A large-scale vaccination effort followed, and by January 2022,
70.0% of HICS participants had been vaccinated (78.5% of adults, Figure 1B).

Protection from reinfection increased with the number of prior infections, and somewhat with the
severity of the outcome (all RT-PCR-confirmed, symptomatic, and moderate/severe infections), although
confidence intervals were wider for more severe outcomes. The highest protection was observed in
those with three+ prior infections against moderate/severe disease (0.19, 95%CI: 0.05-0.79), and the
lowest protection—0.52 (95%CI: 0.36-0.76)—was against all RT-PCR-confirmed infections in those with
one prior infection versus uninfected individuals (Figure 1 & Supplemental Tables 3&5).

The incidence of symptomatic infections was 14.1, 9.2, 5.9, and 4.8 cases per 100 PY for those with 0,
1, 2, and 3+ prior infections (Figure 1C), corresponding to incidence rate ratios (IRRs) of 0.39 (95%CI: 0.26-
0.61), 0.24 (0.13-0.42), and 0.20 (0.09-0.42) for those with 1, 2, and 3+ versus no prior infections (Figure
1D). For moderate/severe disease, incidence was 5.4, 2.8, 1.9, and 1.2 cases per 100 PY in those with 0,
1, 2, and 3+ prior infections, corresponding to IRRs of 0.26 (95%CI: 0.12-0.57), 0.23 (0.08-0.66), and 0.19
(0.05-0.79) for those with 1, 2, and 3+ versus 0 prior infections.

To further assess whether additional prior infections provided incremental protection, we compared
participants with ≥1 and ≥2 prior infections (Supplemental Figure 3). As shown in Supplemental Figure 3
A.1 & A.2, participants with two or more prior infections had significantly lower risk of RT-PCR-
confirmed infection compared to those with only one prior infection (IRRs of 0.61 [0.48-0.77] for 2 vs 1;
and 0.41 [0.26-0.63] for 3+ vs 1); protection also remained significant for 3+ vs 2 prior infections (IRR:
0.60 [0.38-0.93]). Similarly, we observed reduced risk of symptomatic infection for participants with 2 or
3+ infections compared to those with one (IRRs: 0.61 [0.46-0.82] and 0.47 [0.28-0.78], respectively).
However, the number of prior infections was not significantly associated with the risk of moderate or
severe disease (e.g. IRR for 2 vs 1 prior infection: 0.86 [0.52-1.44]) or symptomatic infection when
restricting to participants with ≥2 prior infections (IRR: 0.81 [0.48-1.34]). These findings suggest that
multiple prior infections enhance protection against reinfection, although these associations are weaker
and less precise when examining more severe outcomes.

Similarly, reinfections were less severe than first infections (Figure 2 & Supplemental Tables 4&6),
though with no apparent additional benefit from increasing number of prior infections as seen with
protection from infection. The proportion of moderate/severe disease decreased from 31.5% to 21.5%
to 21.2% in first, second, and third+ infections (Figure 2B), corresponding to relative severities of 0.65
(95%CI: 0.49-0.86) and 0.70 (95%CI: 0.45-1.09) for second and third+ versus first infections (Figure 2C).
Meanwhile, the proportion of subclinical infections increased from 17.3% to 29.9% to 31.0% in first,
second, and third+ infections, corresponding to increased relative severities of 1.57 (95%CI: 1.15-2.16)
and 1.71 (95%CI: 1.11-2.62) for second and third+ infections versus first infections.

Because there are many potentially confounding factors, and for transparency, we have included
Supplemental Figure 4, which shows partially and alternately adjusted models for the main protection
and severity analyses. While all models produced qualitatively similar point estimates indicating
protection, not all models yielded statistically significant associations. In particular, when time since
prior infection or vaccination was included as a covariate, confidence intervals widened and some
estimates were no longer statistically significant (Supplemental Figure S4). For severity analyses,
estimates remained generally similar across model specifications. This stability suggests that variables
that confound infection risk (such as time since infection or vaccination) are not strong confounders of
severity in our community-based cohort once infection has occurred. Additional adjustment for these
variables increased uncertainty (wider confidence intervals) without materially changing the point
estimates, so the simpler model was retained for the main severity analyses.

Stratifying by year (Supplemental Figure 5), we again observed increasing protection with each
subsequent reinfection for 2021 and 2022, however incidence was much lower in 2023 and 2024, and
there were so few first infections in those years that we did not observe protection for 2023 or 2024
(Supplemental Figure 5 & Supplemental Table 7). Reductions in disease severity were apparent in the
pre-Omicron period, but not during Omicron (Supplemental Figure 6 & Supplemental Table 8). During
the pre-Omicron period, second infections were associated with 0.56 (95%CI: 0.40-0.79) times as much
moderate/severe disease and 1.95 (95%CI: 1.33-2.85) times more subclinical infections versus first
infections.

Additionally, the period-of- and time-since- last infection were associated with protection from
reinfection, and, to a lesser extent, severity (Supplemental Figure 7). As expected, protection was
highest when the prior infection matched the circulating variant, and was more recent. Looking at
period of last infection, the highest protection was observed in the pre-Omicron period for those with a
prior pre-Omicron infection (IRR: 0.04, 95%CI: 0.02-0.09 for symptomatic infection) and in the Omicron
era for those with a prior Omicron infection (IRR: 0.06, 95%CI: 0.04-0.09 for any PCR-confirmed
infection). For time since last infection, protection was highest pre-Omicron, for those whose last
infection was 0-180 days prior (IRR of 0.02, 95%CI: 0.00-0.11 for moderate/severe infection). Protection
remained present even for participants with original SARS-CoV-2 infections and infections ≥1 year prior.
For example, during the pre-Omicron era, protection against symptomatic infection for participants with
an original SARS-CoV-2 infection, the IRR was 0.31 (95%CI: 0.25-0.40), and for those with an infection 1-
2 years prior, the IRR was 0.59 (95%CI: 0.45- 0.78). We cannot explain the observed increase in
protection among people with prior infections ≥2 years earlier compared to with those infected 1-2
years earlier, though this may reflect chance variation, differences in variants, or selection effects such
as survivor bias, where those with more durable immunity (e.g., better mucosal immunity) remain
uninfected for longer.

Protection results were largely similar for age groups 18+, 10-17, and 0-9 years (Supplemental Figure 8),
with weaker associations for the youngest children. Likewise, relative severity of reinfection
(Supplemental Figure 9) was similar for adults and older children, but there was no association for the
youngest children.

---

## Methods

Ethics Statement
This study was approved by the institutional review boards at the Nicaraguan Ministry of Health and the
University of Michigan (HUM00119145 and HUM00178355 and CIRE code # NIC-MINSA/CNDR CIRE-
05/04/17-080 Rev 13). Informed consent or parental permission was obtained for all participants.
Assent was obtained from children aged ≥6 years.

The Household Influenza Cohort Study (HICS)
HICS is an ongoing household cohort study with an embedded household transmission study, located in
district II of Managua, Nicaragua. The neighborhoods in district II range from low to middle class,
including several areas classified as urban slums. It was started in 2017 to study influenza, and in 2020
SARS-CoV-2 was added. Regular blood samples are collected for all cohort participants, twice yearly in
2020 and 2021, then yearly thereafter. The transmission study is activated when a household member
becomes sick and tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR after seeking care at the study health clinic.
Activated households are visited by study staff regularly, at approximately days 0, 3, 7, 14, 21, and 30,
for collection of respiratory samples and symptom diaries from all household members, regardless of
symptoms.

Laboratory Assays
Blood samples were tested as paired serum samples (current vs baseline) using an enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assays (ELISAs) protocol adapted from the Krammer laboratory 20. The SARS-CoV-2 spike
receptor binding domain (RBD), spike, and nucleoprotein (NP) proteins for ELISAs were produced in
single batches at the Life Sciences Institute at the University of Michigan; these were generated based
on the original SARS-CoV-2 strain. RBD was used for screening (positive/negative) as it is more specific
than spike, and spike was used to titer samples that screened positive by RBD ELISA; NP ELISAs were also
run, to distinguish between vaccine and infection responses. Real-time reverse-transcription polymerase
chain reaction (RT-PCR) was performed according to the protocol from Chu et al. 21.
All RT-PCR and most ELISAs were performed at the Nicaraguan National Virology Laboratory, with a
minority of 2020 annual samples processed at the University of Michigan.

Infection histories
We used positive serology screens, antibody titer values, 4-fold rises in titer, and RT-PCR positivity to
define first and secondary infections, as outlined in Supplemental Figure 1. To be defined as an
infection, serological samples must have been from participants at least 6 months of age, to avoid
incorrectly classifying maternal immunity, and first infections serologically detected by RBD screen or
spike titer must have been before the first COVID vaccination. We estimated the date of serologically-
defined infections to be the median between samples, or for positive screens, we used the median of
the sample date and March 1, 2020 or the participant’s birthday if they were born after 2020 or a
previous negative sample date. RT-PCR-detected infections must have been ≥60 days apart from each
other. Infection sequences based on serology were required to have a longer time span between
infections than those involving a PCR-detected infection given the inherent uncertainty in the exact
timing of serologically-detected infections. Distinct infections detected serologically must have been ≥6
months apart from each other. Paired serology samples that spanned a vaccination event or were
collected soon after vaccination were excluded, as the resulting antibody rise likely reflects vaccine-
induced immunity rather than infection. Sequential infections detected by RT-PCR and 4-fold rise must
have occurred >90 days apart from each other. Any potential infections within 60 days of each other
were flagged for manual inspection.

Severity
Severity was evaluated only for RT-PCR-confirmed infections, as symptom diaries and clinic records were
only available exclusively for these infections. Symptoms reported in daily symptom diaries and clinic
visits were used to define severity, as severe (hospitalized, doctors say they should have been
hospitalized, or death), moderate (lower respiratory symptoms or overall poor condition), mild (loss of
smell/taste, fever, or ≥2 symptoms), or subclinical (≤1 symptom not meeting definitions for higher
severity).

Main Exposures and Outcomes
For protection analyses, all prior infections detected serologically and by RT-PCR were used to define the
exposure, and the outcome was incident RT-PCR-detected infections with defined severity. Severity
analyses were restricted to RT-PCR-detected infections only; the exposure for severity analyses was
infection number (1st, 2nd, 3rd+), and the outcome was severity.

Vaccination
Vaccines (Covishield 19) were available to elderly or high-risk individuals starting in early 2021. In the fall
of 2021, vaccinations became much more widely available, including Sputnik V, Sputnik Light,
AstraZeneca, Abdala, Soberana, Pfizer, Janssen, Sinopharm, and Moderna. Vaccination status was
defined as unvaccinated, partially vaccinated, fully vaccinated (number of doses varied by vaccine;
Sputnik light only required one dose for full vaccination), or boosted; we counted vaccines that occurred
at least 14 days prior. Vaccines targeting the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid were not counted with the
vaccinated groups (only a few people have had a vaccine targeting the nucleocapsid, starting in 2023).

Analysis
While new households were recruited in 2023 to maintain the cohort size, participants were limited to
those enrolled before January 1, 2021 or were born into the cohort (enrolled before age 1y) so that full
infection histories would be known. Person-time, for the protection analysis, included all weeks in the
study period when participants were enrolled, excluding the period immediately following infection. We
excluded up to 52 days post-infection, as this was the shortest interval at which a new infection was
detected in the cohort due to our infection definition. Person-time for an individual changed exposure
categories as new immune events occurred.
Poisson regression and mixed effect Poisson regression models were used to calculate relative risks (RR),
using the glm (base R) and glmer (lme4 package version 1.1-37) functions in R. Percent protection was
calculated as (1- RR)*100. We stratified all analyses by age (0-9y, 10-17y, and 18+y). We also stratified
by year or period, to account for high vaccination rates starting around November 2021 and differences
in variants.

Covariates
For model adjustment, we considered vaccination status (none, partial, full, and boosted), age (in years),
sex, days since last infection and vaccination (both categorized as ‘uninfected/unvaccinated’, [0-14),
[14-49) [vaccination only], then increments of 60 days until [870-2000]), year or period (original SARS-CoV-2,
pre-Omicron variant, and Omicron), and household clustering (as a mixed effect). Not all variables could
be included in stratified analyses. Examples of model specification are shown in Supplementary Tables 3
& 4.

1. A general limitation of the analysis is that it does not account for sex, and age, which are known to be two key determinants of disease outcome. Additionally, household clustering is probably also important to account for in order for the statistical inference to be correct.

### Reviewer 2

General
This is a research article by Dr. Maier and colleagues comparing the protection of infection-acquired immunity from single vs multiple prior infections against symptomatic infection and clinical severity. The study concludes that infection-acquired immunity against symptomatic infection increases with each subsequent infection and that clinical severity declines with each subsequent infection. The study leverages a household cohort study from Managua, Nicaragua collecting routine serologic testing and symptom-triggered PCR testing over the entire Covid-19 pandemic period (2000-2024). This cohort design and dataset is an impressive strength of the article, given the complete individual histories of vaccination and prior infection based on the longitudinal design; this level of detailed data is rare. However, the current analytic structure has some methodological issues that preclude meaningful interpretation of the study findings in their present form. First, the analysis does not appear to account for timing since the last infection – however we know infection-acquired immunity wanes. This results in downward biasing of the estimate for protection generated by a single infection (which has a longer period of follow up, presumably after substantial waning of protection) compared to protection generated by a second or third infection (with shorter period of follow up, presumably during a period of higher protection before waning). Second, the findings of lower clinical severity from repeated infections could also be explained by both differences in which variants are circulating during 1st vs 2nd vs 3rd infection (and variant-specific clinical severity) and not accounting for waning of protection. Third, there may be differential indirect protection on the household level that is affecting these direct protection estimates. As the number of prior infections increases, so does the immunity of the household members, which may confound measure of direct protection (providing more indirect protection over time in households with members with higher number of prior infections, which could confound the direct protection measures). Finally, the statistical analysis and data processing could be more clearly described to better understand the analysis. I hope my comments can be constructive, as most of my concerns can be addressed and the scientific question and study are both important and interesting.
Major
--Accounting for timing since last infection / waning in protection: It is well established that protection from infection-acquired immunity wanes over time, whether due to immune-mediated mechanisms or due to increasing mismatch of host immune response and evolving viral variants. Therefore, an analysis comparing protection from different numbers of infections needs to account for timing since last infection to account for this waning of protection. The current main analysis does not appear to do so, which will bias the estimates, especially for single infection persons that have a longer follow up period (likely with substantial waning of protection) compared to the two or three infection participants with a relatively shorter follow up period (where protection will be stronger). This is evidenced in the authors’ supplemental analysis. For example, a person with single infection induced protection may have their next infection up to >3 years later, compared to a participant with triple infection induced protection which would have their next infection within 1-2 years. Therefore, is the lower protection from single infection compared to multiple infections due to differences in the immunity or simply timing since last infection? This should be rigorously addressed to determine the validity of the study findings, which currently focus on number of infections rather than timing since last infection. This issue also affects the analysis on clinical severity, which may once again bias downwards protection from single infection due to not accounting for timing since the last infection. The authors could create categories of timing of their prior infection states or perform a more sophisticated rolling matching process (i.e., match 1 vs 0 prior infections over defined time period, match 2 vs 0 prior infections, etc). These proposed approaches each have some challenges (e.g., needing to have overlapping time periods between different immune statuses), but this concern can likely be mostly addressed with additional analysis and should be featured in the main analysis.
--Clinical severity analysis methodological questions: From the current analysis, it is not entirely clear whether clinical severity is lower due to the protection generated from multiple infections or due to the variants affecting these different prior infection groups (e.g., variants circulating when participants have 1 vs 2 vs 3 infections are different). This is partially addressed by their pre- and post-omicron period analysis, but further work could be done to answer this question. As one potential approach, the authors could perform rolling matching to follow matched participants over the same variant periods (ideally more fine scale than just pre- and post-omicron), while accounting for timing of prior infection and vaccine differences. Alternatively, the authors could also highlight this as a limitation (including in the Abstract) if the sample size does not permit. Furthermore, the abstract mentions only comparing clinical severity of PCR+ cases, however the authors should also account for any differences in the fraction of asymptomatic infection (given their serology data) between 1 vs 2 vs 3 prior infection to answer this question about clinical severity.
--Confounding from indirect protection: Prior studies have shown that both Covid-19 vaccines and infection-acquired immunity generate indirect protection, reducing risk of infection to nearby social contacts. The current analysis may be affected by this, given that cases with 3+ infections likely co-reside with household members with high immunity, which may falsely appear as higher direct protection to the case, whereas it’s actually due to the indirect protection from the household members. Given the impressive household cohort study done by the authors, this could be directly evaluated and accounted for in the analysis based on data availability.
--Description of methods: The methods section is a bit sparse, which makes it more challenging to follow. The following would help: formal specification of the statistical model, relevant covariates, definition of person-time, treatment of repeated individuals (same participant in different immune categories), censoring, data processing, relevant reporting checklists. Discussion on why the authors did not use time-to-event modeling and matching. Does subclinical infection refer to PCR+ case with only one symptom or serologic asymptomatic cases or both?

--Sensitivity analysis: The main analysis focuses on “symptomatic infection” but do the results hold for any infection (asymptomatic + symptomatic)?
Minor
--Consider revised title, “Infection-acquired protection against SARS-CoV-2 symptomatic infection and clinical severity by number of prior infections”
--Abstract: Consider reporting relative risk rather than percentage increases.
--Writing: Would prepare an Introduction vs Results section, rather than a single section (which basically lacks an Introduction). I would consider reworking the Introduction to focus more on addressing prior literature and the key scientific gap this study aims to fill.
Thank you for the opportunity to review this interesting study.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
